source: NCERT Class VII, Social and Political Life II, Polity Ch. 7.

sections.heading: 1. A Shirt's Journey
points: The chapter follows a **cotton shirt** from the **farmer's field to the shop**, revealing a long **chain of markets** and people.
Chain: **cotton farmer → trader → spinning/weaving factory → garment maker → exporter → foreign shop → consumer**.
At each step value is added, but the **gains are shared very unequally**.

sections.heading: 2. The Cotton Farmer at Kurnool
points: The **cotton farmer** often takes a **loan** for seeds/fertiliser and must **repay it after harvest**.
He usually sells to a **local trader** to whom he is in **debt**, at a **low price** (a form of dependence) — earning very little.
Farmers have **little bargaining power** in this arrangement.

sections.heading: 3. The Weavers of Erode and the 'Putting-out' System
points: In the **cloth market at Erode (Tamil Nadu)**, **merchants** control the trade.
Under the **putting-out system**, merchants supply **yarn** to **weavers** and collect the **finished cloth**; weavers work at home but **earn low wages** and bear the risk.
Weavers depend on merchants for both raw material and sale — leaving them **little profit**.

sections.heading: 4. Who Gains the Most
points: The **garment exporters** (supplying foreign brands) and **foreign businesspersons** make the **largest profits**; they keep costs low by paying workers little.
**Workers in garment factories** (often women, employed on a **temporary** basis) get **low wages** and insecure jobs.
So the people who **do the most work** (farmers, weavers, workers) earn the **least**; those who control the market earn the most — an **unequal, unfair** distribution.

sections.heading: 5. High-Yield One-Liners (Last-Minute Recall)
points: Shirt chain: cotton farmer → trader → weaver → garment factory → exporter → foreign shop → consumer.
Cotton farmers (Kurnool) sell cheap to traders they owe money to → earn little.
Putting-out system (Erode): merchants supply yarn, collect cloth; weavers earn low wages.
Exporters & foreign brands gain the most; workers (often women, temporary) earn the least.
Those who work hardest earn least → unequal market.

sections.heading: 6. Common Traps (Watch Out)
points: In the **putting-out system**, merchants provide **yarn** and take the **finished cloth** — weavers bear risk for low pay.
The **biggest profit** goes to **exporters/foreign brands**, not the farmer or weaver.
Cotton farmers' low earnings stem from **debt** and **weak bargaining power**.
The chapter's message: market gains are **unequally** distributed.
